adaptation_notes: The Arabic 'ʿAbd al-Samīʿ' was borrowed orally into Yorùbá speech. 'Samīʿ' (سَمِيع) became 'Semiu' through vowel fronting (ā→e) and the addition of a final vowel (common in Yorùbá phonotactics, which disfavours word-final consonants). 'ʿAbd al-' was resyllabified as 'Abdul'.
An alternative Yorùbá spelling retaining the 'a' vowel closer to the Arabic original. Both 'Abdulsamiu' and 'Abdulsemiu' map to the same canonical name.
A shortened form of Abdulsemiu, common in Yorùbá Muslim communities.

The Arabic 'Sulaymān' (سُلَيْمَان) lost the final nasalised long vowel (ān→on) and gained an open 'o' characteristic of Yorùbá, because Yorùbá syllables tend to be open (CV). The diphthong 'ay' was retained as 'ai'.
A more standard English/West African spelling of the same Arabic name Sulaymān. The final ān is retained as 'an'. Common in written forms and official documents.
A Yorùbá rendering influenced by the English 'Solomon'. The diphthong was collapsed and the 'u' became 'o'. This form is occasionally used but is further from the Arabic original.
The Arabic 'Ibrāhīm' (إِبْرَاهِيم) was adapted with a doubled 'ee' to represent the long vowel ī. This spelling is extremely common in Yorùbá Muslim communities and Nigerian official documents.
Standard transliteration used across the Muslim world. The long ī is written as a single 'i' without the gemination. Both 'Ibrahim' and 'Ibraheem' refer to the same Arabic name.
The Arabic 'ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz' is often shortened to just 'Azeez' in Yorùbá usage. The 'ʿAbd al-' prefix is dropped entirely, which is a common Yorùbá pattern — the name is reduced to the epithet alone.
Full form retained but the ī in Azīz shortened to 'i'. Common in official documents and more formal contexts.

The Arabic 'Fawziyyah' (فَوْزِيَّة) underwent significant phonological change. The diphthong 'aw' became 'ao' (representing the Yorùbá open-o sound). The feminine suffix '-iyyah' collapsed to '-at', a common Yorùbá rendering of Arabic feminine -at/ah endings.
Alternative spelling of Faosat using 'au' rather than 'ao' to represent the Arabic diphthong 'aw'. Equally common in Yorùbá Muslim families.

The Arabic 'Maryam' (مَرْيَم) passed through Hausa and then Yorùbá oral transmission, gaining the diminutive/affectionate suffix '-o' common in Yorùbá. The 'ary' metathesised to 'ori' and an 'a' was inserted for syllable structure, giving 'Moriam' and then 'Moriamo'.
More direct adaptation of 'Maryam', with 'y' becoming 'i' (a standard Yorùbá consonant substitution). Used by both Muslim and Christian Yorùbá families.

The Arabic 'Rāḍiyah' (رَاضِيَة) lost the emphatic ḍ (which has no Yorùbá equivalent) and was replaced with 'l', a more sonorous consonant. The '-iyyah' suffix again collapsed to '-at'. The long ā was shortened.

The Arabic 'Shakūr' (شُكُور) was borrowed into Yorùbá as 'Sikiru'. The 'sh' was simplified to 's' (Yorùbá lacks the 'sh' phoneme in indigenous words). The long ū became 'u', and the vowels shifted under Yorùbá vowel harmony rules.

The Arabic 'Muṭīʿ' (مُطِيع) adapted into Yorùbá as 'Mutiu'. The emphatic ṭ was replaced with the plain 't'. The ī vowel collapsed, and the final ʿ (ayin) — a pharyngeal consonant absent in Yorùbá — was dropped, replaced with the open vowel 'u'.

The Arabic 'Ramaḍān' (رَمَضَان) was adapted as a female name 'Ramota' in Yorùbá. The emphatic ḍ shifted to 't', the ān suffix became 'a', and the name was feminised. Common for girls born during Ramadan.
Direct transliteration of the Arabic month name, used as a personal name. The emphatic ḍ is typically written as plain 'd'.
The Arabic 'Ḥafṣah' (حَفْصَة) adapted into the Yorùbá '-at' suffix pattern. The 'ḥ' (voiceless pharyngeal fricative) is realised as plain 'h'. Extremely common in Yorùbá Muslim families.
The Arabic 'ʿAbdullāh' adapted with the addition of a final 'i', a Hausa/Fulani suffix that has spread into Nigerian Muslim naming conventions across ethnic groups.
Standard transliteration of ʿAbdullāh used across the Muslim world. Very common in formal written contexts.
The Arabic 'Ṣafiyyah' (صَفِيَّة) adapted into the Yorùbá '-at' pattern. The emphatic ṣ became plain 's'. The doubled '-iyyah' suffix collapsed to '-iat' then '-at'.

The Arabic 'Khadījah' (خَدِيجَة) adopted the Yorùbá '-at' ending, giving 'Khadijat'. The kh consonant (a velar fricative) is retained in Yorùbá spelling though often pronounced as 'k' or 'h' in local speech.
The Arabic 'Muṣṭafā' (مُصْطَفَى) spelled with 'ph' instead of 'f' — an older digraph used in West African and colonial-era romanisations of Arabic names. The emphatic ṭ became plain 't'.
Modern standard transliteration of Muṣṭafā. Both 'Mustapha' and 'Mustafa' are in common use in Yorùbá Muslim communities.
The 'ay' diphthong in Zaynab is represented as 'ai' — standard across much of the Muslim world. Very common spelling in Nigerian official documents.
